red_flags: Fever with rigors on top of colic — infected obstructed kidney (pus under pressure); urgent surgical referral
First-ever 'renal colic' over 60 with hypotension or a pulsatile mass — ruptured aortic aneurysm until proven otherwise; urgent surgical referral
Anuria, or colic in a solitary or transplanted kidney — obstruction is losing the only kidney
Painless visible hematuria with weight loss — urinary tract malignancy until excluded
Severe unremitting pain with vomiting and rising creatinine
exam: Record temperature, BP, and pulse — fever with tachycardia flags the obstructed infected kidney
Press over the renal angle for tenderness
Palpate the abdomen deliberately for an expansile pulsatile mass — mandatory in every first presentation over 60
Feel femoral pulses on both sides
Palpate for a ballotable loin mass — renal tumor or gross hydronephrosis
Percuss for a distended bladder — outflow obstruction with retention
Examine the spine: palpate vertebrae and test flexion/extension — reproduction of pain on movement supports a musculoskeletal cause
Inspect the flank skin in good light for vesicular rash in a dermatomal band
Examine the external genitalia — referred testicular pain is common, and a torted testis can present as groin/loin pain
Elicit Murphy's sign for right-sided pain — biliary colic mimics renal colic

investigations.why: Microscopic hematuria supports stone disease; nitrites and pyuria support pyelonephritis; a completely normal dipstick weakens both and pushes toward musculoskeletal, biliary, or vascular causes
Leukocytosis supports pyelonephritis or an infected obstructed system; anemia raises renal tumor or a bleeding aneurysm
Creatinine defines whether obstruction is threatening renal function — critical in a single kidney — and is needed before any contrast study
First-line: hydronephrosis rules in obstruction, a renal mass rules in tumor, and the same scan screens the aorta in older patients
Shows the majority of urinary stones (radio-opaque) and gives a baseline to follow the stone; radiolucent stones will be missed, so a negative film does not exclude
Markedly raised supports pyelonephritis or infected obstruction over uncomplicated stone colic
Confirms and types urinary infection when dipstick is positive — separates pyelonephritis from sterile stone hematuria
